extracted.subtask_description: Wire-service news reporting (Associated Press) from the mid-20th century covering international & domestic developments, government decisions, technical reports, and human-interest items. The copy is aimed at general newspaper readers and editors assembling news pages.

rubrics_metrics.name: State secrets definition and penalties
rubrics_metrics.description: State secrets were defined as 'consisting of information and documents or other material which, for reasons of defense, security or other paramount economic or political interests of the Polish state or states on terms of friendship with the Polish state, may be made exclusively accessible only to persons authorized to receive such information.' The new decree provides maximum penalties up to fifteen years' imprisonment for activities detrimental to the security of the people's state.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Published in Nowe Drogi and signed by the council of ministers headed by President Boleslaw Bierut; intended to protect Polish state secrets. The decree lists categories of people (visiting journalists, scientists, sportsmen, artists, men of letters and some other persons) who might be controlled/used in espionage contexts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Joint command-post site selection considerations
rubrics_metrics.description: Factors to consider when deciding where and how to build a joint command post (a protected military/government command center) if the Pentagon came under air attack.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: List of considerations includes: vital communication links (easy access to existing telephone and telegraph lines, preferably trunk lines underground); natural caverns or mines with thick overhead protection are desirable; proximity to trunk communication lines; availability of technical information on underground construction; the Appalachian Mountains region (within a few hundred miles of Washington) cited as having useful natural features; the site may be midcontinent or in a mountain region and need not be in a single region; some projects would require Congressional appropriation. The study moved from preliminary into detailed planning and noted funds/approvals would be necessary.

rubrics_metrics.name: National capital vulnerabilities to atomic attack
rubrics_metrics.description: Specific geographic and structural features that make the national capital (Washington) especially vulnerable to atomic bombing.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enumerated vulnerabilities: (1) radar bomb-sighting aided by clear Potomac river images allows pinpointing of buildings via triangulation; (2) the Pentagon's steel-and-concrete construction gives good radar delineation; (3) downtown and adjacent areas lie in a broad shallow bowl with few ridges to reduce blast effect; (4) major government buildings are strung in a straight line from southeast to northwest (Capitol to White House), making a straight bombing run effective; (5) three bridges including the only eastern rail link between northern and southern sections are within a narrow zone; (6) two military airfields (Bolling and Anacostia) and National Airport are clustered together. These observations are cited to argue the capital is a 'bombardier's dream.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Shelter protection design principles (Tribune Tower example)
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles and practical measures used by the Chicago Tribune in designing in-building shelters to protect employees and tenants against atomic blast, heat and radiological penetration (short of a direct hit).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Atomic scientists advised planners that shelters would 'afford good protection' provided the bomb did not hit within a 'crucial radius' and that direct hits were not assumed survivable. Design guidance included: 'get as much mass as you can between you and the explosion'; use of heavy newsprint rolls to reinforce shelter walls; relying on outer walls with substantial mass (reference to seven inches of steel and limestone in the tower's outer walls); distribution of shelter areas (30 shelter areas for ~3,900 people); practical notes on roll size and weight for moving into shelters. The plan was reviewed by scientists and adjusted for practicality (e.g., roll dimensions and weights).

rubrics_metrics.name: Atomic bomb injury severity by distance (medical assessment)
rubrics_metrics.description: Medical assessment of expected severity of injuries at various distances from an atomic explosion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Summary of the specialist's statements: very severe / lethal effects within about 1 mile (few survivors among those exposed in that radius); from about 1 to 2 miles many serious injuries would be expected; between about 2 and 3 miles injuries might occur but most would not be serious; beyond about 3 miles there would be relatively few injuries. The assessment emphasizes destructive blast effects producing large numbers of casualties rather than lingering radiological injury.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural steps for obtaining U.S. radio/broadcast equipment abroad
rubrics_metrics.description: Reported procedural requirements and approvals involved when a foreign government or entity seeks U.S. radio equipment or replacement parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Negotiations for U.S.-manufactured radio equipment would take considerable time and involve multiple steps: a bid, approval from the manufacturer's home office, a recommendation from the U.S. embassy in the purchasing country, and State Department approval. This was noted in the context of Yugoslavia seeking Western replacement parts after eastern supply sources were cut off.
